What is a Stroke?

Strokes are one of the most misunderstood and myth-ridden major health conditions. Where misconceptions such as; Strokes are always painful, occur in the heart, are inevitable and cannot be prevented, and is a condition only seen in the elderly can limit awareness and understanding of strokes among young people (Lennon, 2022).

 

425,000 Australians reported experiencing a stroke at some point during their lifetime in 2022. Whilst strokes accounted for 7900 Australian deaths in 2024 (Australian Institute of Health and Welfare [AIHW], 2026). Globally, Strokes are the second leading cause of death for aged 60+ and the fifth leading cause of those aged 15-59. (Feigin, V. L., 2025). A stroke occurs when blood supply to a brain region is unachievable typically through a blocked or ruptured blood vessel. This results in brain damage, disability or death. Despite stroke risk increasing with age, it is important to recognise that all ages can be affected. Additionally long-term habits contribute to the development of stroke symptoms (Lennon, 2022).

Stroke Classification Categories

Ischemic Stroke

Accounting for 87% of strokes globally, Ischemic strokes occur when arterial blood flow is severely reduced or cut off, causing permanent brain damage and death. When a large amount of brain cells die, they lose their ability to control the corresponding bodily function. Ischemic strokes are mainly caused by blood clots. They are the most common cause of stroke in younger age demographics (Cleveland Clinic, 2024).

Haemorrhagic Stroke

Accounts for roughly 13% of strokes globally, Haemorrhagic strokes occur when a weakened blood vessel ruptures. It bleeds into the surrounding brain where blood is then accumulated and compresses the brain tissue (American Stroke Association [ASA], 2026).

The two common types are intracerebral haemorrhage, which occurs within the brain, and subarachnoid haemorrhage, which occurs between the inner and outer layers of tissue surrounding the brain. These strokes are mainly caused by hypertension and high blood pressure (Healthdirect, 2026).

Transient Ischemic Attack (TIA) – Mini Stroke

Caused by a temporary blockage of blood flow to the brain, but doesn’t result in permanent damage, typically lasting only a few minutes. Often seen as a warning for a future stroke, this is seen in 1 in 3 people (Mayo Clinic, 2026).

Risk Factors and Prevention

Risk Factors

Risk Factor

Type

How it increases stroke risk

Age

Non-modifiable

Blood vessels weaken with age, and conditions such as hypertension become more probable

Sex

Non-modifiable

Males, pregnant and post-partum females have an increased stroke risk

Family History/Genetics

Non-modifiable

Inherited genetic factors may increase stroke risk

Previous TIA

Non-modifiable

A TIA may indicate underlying vascular problems and increase future stroke possibility

Hypertension (High Blood Pressure)

Modifiable

Damages artery walls and increases chance of blood vessel rupture or blood clots

Type 2 Diabetes (T2DM)

Modifiable

Glucose is difficult to absorb which damages blood vessels, consequently increasing risk of blood clots

High Cholesterol

Modifiable

Creates plaque build-up on arteries, which narrows them and thus are prone to blockage

Atrial Fibrillation (AF)

Modifiable

Irregular heartbeat causes constant blood flow, thus increased chance of clots which travel towards the brain

Inactivity

Modifiable

Increases risk of hypertension, T2DM, and high cholesterol

Unhealthy diet

Modifiable

May contribute to T2DM, high cholesterol and hypertension

Smoking

Modifiable

Damaged vessels, and raised blood pressure, increasing probability of clots

Chronic Stress

Modifiable

Contributes to hypertension and unhealthy behaviours

Alcohol

Modifiable

Excessive consumption can lead to AF and hypertension

Prevention

80% of strokes are preventable (Stroke Foundation, 2026). Lifestyle changes and effective hypertension management can marginally reduce stroke risk.  To reduce your chance of a stroke you can:

-       Reduce smoking and passive smoking

-       Regular physical activity (150 minutes of moderate intensity per week)

-       Limiting alcohol usage

-       Improving air quality

-       Adopting a healthy diet and lifestyle

-       Antihypertension treatment if required

-       Effectively managing other health conditions

Using the following table, you may calculate a PREDICTED likelihood of experiencing a stroke:

0-4: Very low risk

5-9: Moderate risk

10-13: High risk

14+: Very high risk

Symptoms

Short-term Symptoms

The core short-term stroke symptoms are recognised through the acronym BE-FAST (Figure 2) (Cleveland Clinic, 2025,) These symptoms appear during and immediately after an Ischaemic stroke. Neuron functioning slows down within the first 5 seconds of the blockage. By 30 minutes the neurons are deprived of oxygen, glucose. There becomes an overactivity of calcium and Microglia, causing fluids and plasma to leak into the brain tissue, which subsequently induces these symptoms (Salaudeen et al., 2024).

Blocked arteries reduce blood flow into the brain, decreasing oxygen and glucose transport. This reduces ATP production through oxidative phosphorylation, causing sodium-potassium pumps to fail and disrupt neuronal electrical signalling (Figure 3). Sodium accumulates inside neurons, resulting in water entering by osmosis and produce cellular swelling (cytotoxic oedema) (Yang et al., 2019).

Vision and balance problems – Impaired signalling in the visual cortex disrupts visual processing, while dysfunction in the cerebellum or vestibular pathways affects balance and coordination (Salaudeen et al., 2024).

Face and arm weakness – Reduced influx of oxygen and ATP leads to Ion-pump failure. This disrupts electrical impulses in motor pathways, reducing signals reaching muscles and causing weakness or paralysis (Salaudeen et al., 2024).

Speech difficulties – Impaired neuronal signalling in Broca’s area or Wernicke’s area disrupts speech production or language comprehension (Salaudeen et al., 2024).

Grundy, A. (n.d.). 2 [Figure]. In Finding a neurologist in regional Australia. Brain Foundation.

Long-Term Symptoms

Prolonged ischaemia (reduction in blood flow deprives cells and tissues of oxygen and nutrient) causes ATP decline and excessive glutamate release. Glutamate Excitotoxicity overstimulates N-methyl-D-aspartate (NMDA) receptors, allowing excessive calcium into neurons (Salaudeen, 2024). This activates destructive enzymes that damage proteins, membrane lipids and DNA. Calcium overload also interrupts mitochondrial function and increases reactive oxygen species, causing oxidative stress. These processes contribute to neuronal death through necrosis or apoptosis (Yang et al., 2019).

Damaged cells trigger inflammation which activates microglia and attracts white blood cells. This results in the release of Inflammatory chemicals and enzymes, including matrix metalloproteinases (MMPs) which damage tight-junction proteins in the blood–brain barrier (BBB). Increased BBB permeability allows fluid to leak into brain tissue, causing cerebral oedema and potentially worsen neuronal injury (Yang et al., 2019).

Neuronal death can cause prolonged symptoms. Recovery depends on the extent of brain damage and the brain’s ability to reorganise connections through neuroplasticity (Salaudeen et al, 2024). In young adults, identifying stroke causes can require more intrusive and extensive procedures. Lasting impairments may affect employment, raising a family and driving. Late complications can include anxiety, depression, sleep disorders and movement disorders (Tufts Medicine, 2025). Common Long term symptoms include: Sensory loss and pain, Weakness or paralysis, Memory and concentration issues (Department of Health, n.d).

Dysgraphia: When necrosis and apoptosis occurs in the left angular gyrus, the cellular networks which control spelling is disrupted and overtime becomes lost (Yang et al., 2019).

Emotional lability: Damage to connections between the frontal lobes and limbic structures impairs emotional regulation. Additionally, Glutamine over-excites emotive motor pathways, causing irregular emotional responses (Yang et al., 2019).

Salaudeen, M.A. (2024). 3 [Figure]. In Understanding the Pathophysiology of Ischemic Stroke: The Basis of Current Therapies and Opportunity for New Ones. National Library of Medicine.

Major Treatment options

Medical treatment for strokes can help reduce symptoms but none can repair the brain damage caused by stroke (Majumder, 2024).

Cell-Based Therapy

Cell-based therapies have proven to be effective and a reliable form of treatment, it is a supportive regenerative treatment which aims to reduce brain inflammation, protect surviving neurons, and boost the brain's natural healing processes (Majumder, 2024).

It is injected into the surrounding brain tissue, veins or artery, helping support signal transmission between neurons. However, stem-based therapy is still in developmental stages and is highly invasive (Flint Rehab, 2024).

Activity-Based Therapy

Activity based therapies are typically used for patients which have lost motor function and/or speech. Physiotherapy and Occupational therapy are two main treatments used in recovering from an ischemic stroke (Majumder, 2024).

Both require repeated exercises which allow remaining neural networks to adapt and compensate for previous neuron damage. They are both useful in gaining confidence and improving quality of life, however it takes time and individuals ability to reach maximum recovery varies (Stroke Foundation, 2026).

Drug-Based Therapy

Drug therapies are used to target receptors (ion channels) to help restore neural function and improve blood flow in capillaries with minimal side effects. These are typically the key medical treatments used for recovery (Majumder, 2024).

Thrombolysis (clot dissolving medication) – Thrombolysis (tPA) is medication used to dissolve blood clots which block blood flow to the brain. It is most effective when administered promptly, typically within 4.5 hours of symptoms beginning, after appropriate tests and brain imaging have been completed to confirm the stroke. TPA activates plasminogen into plasmin (an enzyme which breaks down fibrin), which is the protein which forms the blood clot structure. This process dissolves the clot and can restore blood flow, which consequently allows oxygen and glucose to reach affected brain cells. It supports cellular respiration and ATP production whilst preserving viable neurons and limiting further damage (Gravanis et al., 2008). TPA’s are not used in patients which are pregnant, experiencing recent surgery, trauma or strong blood thinning medication (Brain Foundation, 2017;  Majumder, 2024). Although it may restore blood flow and reduce brain tissue damage, the procedure carries a risk of bleeding and is less effective for large clots in major arteries (Brain Foundation, 2017).

Mechanical thrombectomy (endovascular clot retrieval) – A surgical procedure which restores blood flow to the brain and preserves remaining viable neurons (Majumder, 2024). It is performed by inserting a catheter into an artery typically located in the leg or groin. The catheter is guided up to the brain where a device is used to gather the clot (Stroke Foundation. (n.d.). It’s recommended for patients with large clots, proving successful in 80-85% of removals. However, it is invasive and carries risks of bleeding and vessel injury. Recovery depends on the extent and location of brain tissue damage (Brain Foundation, 2017).

Antiplatelet medication – To prevent a further stroke, medication such as aspirin or clopidogrel is used. This is effective early after an ischemic stroke occurs. It limits platelets sticking together which helps limit further clot formation, however does not directly remove existing clots. It imposes high bleeding risks and is a long-term medication which must only be used under prescription via health professionals (Brain Foundation, 2017).

Health Services and Resources

Any type of stroke is a medical emergency. If you or anyone nearby shows signs of a stroke, call Triple Zero (000) immediately, even if symptoms disappear. If seeking information post stroke, the following services are available, offering advice, guidance and support (Cleveland Clinic, 2025).

Lifeline (24/7) 13 11 14

Facts/Statistics

  • 1 in 4 people globally experience a stroke in their lifetime

  • Stroke is one of Australia's biggest killers. having a greater impact than prostate and breast cancer

  • 1.9 million brain cells are affected per minute when a stroke occurs

  • Over the past 20 years, the lifetime risk of stroke has increased by 50%

  • Over 11 million new stroke deaths every year

  • In 2023, a stroke occurred every 11 minutes in Australia

  • Over 60% of strokes happen to those under 70

  • 16% of strokes happen to those under 50

  • Strokes represent 0.66% of Global GDP

  • Globally, the economic impact of stroke is estimated to reach over USD $1 trillion by 2030

(World Stroke Organization, 2026; Stroke Foundation, 2026)
